stimulus.text: When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty; because apprehensions may arise, lest the same monarch or senate should enact tyrannical laws, to execute them in a tyrannical manner. Again, there is no liberty, if the judiciary power be not separated from the legislative and executive. There would be an end of everything, were the same man or the same body, whether of the nobles or of the people, to exercise those three powers.
stimulus.source_note: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748), abridged. Public domain.

stem: How did Montesquieu's idea in this passage most directly shape the government Americans created after independence?

options.text: It led the states to give their governors the power to make laws
options.misconception: Giving governors lawmaking power would unite executive and legislative power — the opposite of Montesquieu's idea.

options.text: It led Congress to elect judges to serve in the legislature
options.misconception: Putting judges in the legislature would unite judicial and legislative power, against Montesquieu's rule.

options.text: It led the Constitution to divide power among legislative, executive, and judicial branches
It led the states to abolish their courts and let legislatures judge cases
options.misconception: Abolishing courts would hand judicial power to the legislature — the union Montesquieu warns against.

rationales.C: Background: the Constitution divides power into three branches, each checking the others — Montesquieu's separation of powers made concrete. The structure, not the virtue of officeholders, guards liberty.
rationales.A: Governors making laws would unite two powers in one hand. Montesquieu's idea points the other way.
rationales.B: Judges sitting in the legislature would merge judicial and legislative power, not separate them.
rationales.D: Letting legislatures judge cases hands them judicial power too. Montesquieu's idea requires courts of their own.
rationales.general:
1. Name Montesquieu's rule. The three powers — legislative, executive, judicial — must sit in separate hands.
2. Look at the Constitution. Background: it creates three branches, one for each power, with checks on one another.
3. Match the idea to the structure. The American division of powers is Montesquieu's principle written into a constitution.
Remember: an idea shapes a government when you can point to the institution that carries it — here, the three branches.
